content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published recommendations in 2013 regarding postnatal care for mothers and newborns. These guidelines emphasize the critical importance of the postnatal period, which is often neglected despite being a time when most maternal and infant deaths occur. The recommendations aim to provide evidence-based practices to improve outcomes for mothers and newborns, particularly in resource-limited settings. 1. Postnatal Care in Health Facilities: If the birth occurs in a health facility, both the mother and newborn should remain under care for at least 24 hours after delivery. If the birth takes place at home, the first postnatal contact should occur within 24 hours. Additional postnatal visits are recommended on day 3 (48–72 hours), between days 7–14, and at six weeks postpartum. 2. Home Visits for Postnatal Care: Home visits during the first week after birth are strongly recommended to ensure the well-being of both the mother and the newborn. This is particularly important in settings where access to health facilities is limited. 3. Exclusive Breastfeeding: All infants should be exclusively breastfed from birth until six months of age. This practice is critical for the health and development of the newborn. 4. Umbilical Cord Care: For newborns born at home in areas with high neonatal mortality rates, the application of 4% chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump during the first week of life is recommended. In low neonatal mortality settings, clean and dry cord care is advised. 5. Delayed Bathing: Bathing of the newborn should be delayed for at least 24 hours after birth. If cultural practices prevent this, bathing should be delayed for at least six hours. The baby should be dressed appropriately for the ambient temperature, with one to two layers of clothing more than adults, and a hat or cap should be used. 6. Rooming-In: Mothers and newborns should not be separated and should remain in the same room 24 hours a day. This promotes bonding and facilitates breastfeeding. 7. Immunization: Immunizations should be promoted according to existing WHO guidelines. 8. Maternal Assessment: During the first 24 hours after birth, postpartum women should undergo regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate. Blood pressure should be measured shortly after birth and again within six hours if normal. Urine voiding should be documented within six hours. 9. Ongoing Maternal Monitoring: Beyond the first 24 hours, subsequent postnatal visits should include assessments of general well-being, urinary and bowel function, perineal wound healing, and any pain or discomfort. Breastfeeding progress should also be evaluated. Emotional well-being, family and social support, and coping strategies should be discussed. Women should be encouraged to report any changes in mood or behavior. 10. Postpartum Depression: At 10–14 days postpartum, women should be asked about the resolution of mild postpartum depression (maternal blues). If symptoms persist, further assessment for postpartum depression should be conducted. 11. Domestic Abuse: Women should be observed for any signs of domestic abuse and provided with information on whom to contact for advice and support. 12. Sexual Health: Women should be asked about the resumption of sexual activity and any associated discomfort (e.g., dyspareunia) as part of their overall well-being assessment during the two to six weeks postpartum period. 13. Counseling: All women should receive information about the physiological recovery process after birth and be advised to report any health concerns to a healthcare professional. Specific signs and symptoms to watch for include postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), pre-eclampsia, and other complications. These recommendations are designed to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes by addressing critical aspects of postnatal care. They are intended for use by healthcare professionals, policymakers, and program managers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The guidelines will be regularly updated as new evidence becomes available, with major reviews occurring at least every five years.
